Original lyrics, sung by four models

240 original song lyrics — 20 genres × 3 length profiles × 4 languages — each rendered by four music models in two conditions: once as a solo voice with nothing else in the file, and once as an ordinary song in its genre. Every model sings exactly the same words from the same caption with the same seed. 1920 of 1920 renders succeeded. All audio 160 kbps stereo.

4models

4 · MiniMax sings German and Spanish with English-sounding phonemes. Language ID on the rendered audio: LeVo 99.4 %, HeartMuLa 100 %, ACE-Step 99.6 %, MiniMax 70.6 %. Its flat en−xx row above should be read with that in mind — it is even across languages partly because it is not fully rendering them.

So: ACE-Step for songs, LeVo for isolated voice. The two questions have different winners, and the reason is architectural rather than a quality gap.

What none of this settles: whether any take is a single voice. A vocal separator leaves a doubled or harmonised second singer inside the vocal stem, so LeVo's 0.000 proves no instruments, not one singer. That needs ears. The aesthetics head also disagrees with the judge on this page (it ranks HeartMuLa first, the judge ranks ACE-Step first); both are printed below and neither is used to filter.

Does LeVo 2's English strength survive translation?

That is the question this page exists to answer, so it is answered first and the evidence follows. Every metric further down is broken out by language and nothing is averaged across the four, because a grand mean is exactly what would hide a model × language interaction.

The multilingual verdict, from the tables below.

By blind judge, overall (0–5), floor 0.39:

  • English: ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (+0.67 over LeVo 2)
  • German: ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (+0.85 over LeVo 2)
  • French: ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (+0.40 over LeVo 2)
  • Spanish: ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (+0.70 over LeVo 2)

By Whisper word F1 against the words given, floor 0.129:

  • English: LeVo 2
  • German: ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (inside the noise floor — call it a tie with LeVo 2)
  • French: HeartMuLa 3B (inside the noise floor — call it a tie with LeVo 2)
  • Spanish: HeartMuLa 3B (inside the noise floor — call it a tie with LeVo 2)

Read these as the summary of the per-language tables, not as a substitute for them: they compress a mean and a spread over dozens of clips into one name. Where a margin is inside the floor the label says so, and a tie is the honest answer there.

One of these four claims is a guarantee. Three are compliance.

LeVo 2's vocals-only take cannot contain an instrument. gen_type='vocal' overwrites the accompaniment codebook with a constant token before the diffusion decoder ever runs, so no instrument can be decoded into the file whatever the caption says. It is a property of the renderer, not of the prompt, and it cannot fail.

HeartMuLa, ACE-Step and MiniMax have no such switch. None of the three exposes a vocals-only render mode; ACE-Step has the opposite switch (instrumental=True) and nothing for this direction. For all three, "vocals only" is a request in the prompt and nothing more — each was given the strongest prompt-only request this project has (a cappella, solo, unaccompanied, no instruments, no backing track, no second voice, no harmony, no choir), and whether it was honoured is an empirical question with a measured answer below, not a claim.

Do not read the two as the same kind of statement. A previous comparison here was misread exactly this way. LeVo's zero is a fact about its decoder; every other number in the accompaniment column is a compliance rate, and a model can lose it on any individual clip. The column is measured, per clip, with BS-Roformer, precisely so that nobody has to take the prompt's word for it.

Statistics

Every metric below is broken out by language. That is the point of the page: the four models are compared inside English, inside German, inside French and inside Spanish, never only as a grand mean, because a grand mean would hide exactly the interaction worth knowing. Each model × language cell holds n = 120 clips (60 lyrics × 2 conditions); the number after ± is the standard deviation across those clips, not a standard error, so it describes the spread of the clips and not the precision of the mean.

Read this before the aesthetics column. The music-aesthetics head has already contradicted human-facing judges badly on this project's own material: it scored a HeartMuLa arm 4.12 that judges scored 0/30, and a LeVo arm 2.41 that judges scored 22/30. It is kept because it is cheap, uniform and reproducible, and because a stored number can be checked later; the standing project rule is that it is stored as a field and never filtered on. Nothing on this page is selected, ranked or hidden by it. Treat it as one signal among several — and where it disagrees with the lyric-intelligibility and language columns, which measure something checkable, prefer those.
And it disagrees on this page, now. Ranked by the aesthetics head, the four arms come out HeartMuLa 3B (3.86) > ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (3.38) > LeVo 2 (2.60) > MiniMax Music 3 (1.64). Ranked by the blind judge on the same clips, they come out ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (4.60) > HeartMuLa 3B (3.98) > LeVo 2 (3.94) > MiniMax Music 3 (0.62). The two orderings are not the same. Nothing on this page resolves that for you; both are printed, per language, and the accompaniment and intelligibility columns — which measure a fact rather than a preference — are the ones to lean on.

The noise floor — what a difference has to beat

Re-scoring a file gives the same number to the last decimal: these heads are deterministic, so a re-scoring noise floor would be exactly zero and would licence any difference at all. The floor that matters is the generator's: the same model, the same caption, the same lyric, a different seed. 160 clips per model — the typical-length profile of all 20 genres, all four languages, both conditions — were rendered a second time for exactly this.

F1 of the transcript's words against the exact lines the model was given: recall falls when the model stops early or slurs, precision falls when it invents. laion/music-popularity-full-ft, reported on its native log1p scale because that is the scale its loss was computed on. Carries the same caveat as the aesthetics head: stored, never filtered on.

One artefact was suspected here and measured rather than assumed. The four arms are not rendered at the same loudness — median RMS runs from 0.269 (LeVo 2, hard-limited to a peak of exactly 1.0 on essentially every file) down to 0.125 (MiniMax) — and Whisper's log-mel front end is an absolute dB scale, so the encoder really does see a different input at a different gain. Re-scoring clips at 0.25×, 0.5× and 1×, and again peak- and RMS-normalised, put a number on it: over a 12 dB swing the aesthetics head moves 0.054 points on average and not even consistently in one direction, against a 2.40-point spread between the arms; the popularity head does move systematically, +0.068 log1p plays per dB, monotonically in 12 of 12 clips. Normalising every clip to a common RMS leaves both rankings bit-for-bit unchanged. Note also that the popularity bias rewards loudness, and LeVo 2 is the loudest arm and still scores lowest — so its near-zero popularity is a property of its audio, not of its gain. The comparison is not a loudness artefact.

MiniMax Music 30.680 ±0.2060.643 ±0.2210.635 ±0.2400.664 ±0.2120.655

BS-Roformer (Viperx ep.317) splits every clip into a vocal and an instrumental stem; the number is the instrumental stem's share of total separated energy. 0.0 is a bare voice, a normal pop mix is 0.5–0.9. The table above pools both conditions; the vocals-only condition on its own is the row that matters and is broken out next.

A low accompaniment fraction does not prove one voice. A vocal separator pulls voice away from instruments; it cannot pull voice away from voice. A clip with a doubled, stacked or harmonised second voice keeps that second voice inside the vocal stem and scores near zero here. So this column is evidence about instruments only, and the diagnostic runs the other way: a take whose character does not change after separation had a genuine second voice, one that cleans up had removable instrumental bleed.

What separation changes — bleed or a second voice

The accompaniment fraction says how much instrumental energy is in a clip. It cannot say whether what remains is one voice. This table runs the diagnostic instead: the aesthetics head is re-run on the separated vocal stem, and the change from the mix is reported. Read the size of the change, not its direction. The head rewards a full mix, so pulling the instruments out of anything that had them lowers the score; what the number reports is how much separable instrumental content was there. A clip whose score barely moves had nothing for the separator to take — and if such a clip nonetheless sounds thick, that thickness is a second voice, which a vocal separator keeps rather than removes.

LeVo 2 is its own control. Its vocals-only takes move by +0.014 when the separator runs, i.e. not at all: there was no accompaniment to remove, which is what the decoder guarantees. Its full-song takes, the same model and the same measurement, move -1.156. The measurement therefore responds when accompaniment is present and stays flat when it is not, in one arm, which is what makes the other three rows readable: their vocals-only takes move nearly as much as their full songs do.

Each model's own English advantage

The interaction, stated directly: within one model, English minus each other language, paired lyric by lyric (the same profile, the same genre, the same condition). A large positive number means that model is markedly better in English than in that language; a number inside its own interval means it is not.

Read this table down a column, not across a row. A single model's English-minus-German gap is confounded: the lyrics are different texts, and Whisper's own accuracy is not equal across the four languages, so part of any gap belongs to the measurement rather than to the model. Both of those confounds are identical for all four models, so they cancel when one model's gap is compared with another's. The clean comparison is the by-language tables above, where the language is held fixed and only the model changes; this table is here to show whether the English advantage is a property of one model or of the whole task.

Where the judge and the aesthetics head disagree, say so rather than pick. Neither is ground truth. The judge hears 45 s of the clip and has a written anchor for every level; the aesthetics head sees 30 s of spectrogram and has already been wrong here by the width of the scale. Both are printed above, per language, so the disagreement is visible instead of resolved by whoever built the page.

Before quoting the MiniMax Music 3 column

The files are written correctly; the runtime is not the served one. This arm scores far below the other three on every axis, so the first question was whether we had broken the audio ourselves. The obvious candidate was the sample rate: the model card says 32 kHz, the checkpoint's vocoder config says 44100, and the files are written at 44100. If those samples were really 32 kHz in a 44.1 kHz container, everything would play 1.38× fast and score exactly like this. It was checked, and the container is right. Three pieces of evidence, any one of which is sufficient: re-reading the same samples at 32 kHz does not recover the words (word F1 goes 0.05 → 0.09, against 0.75 for the other arms, and a LeVo control deliberately mis-read at 32 kHz loses only 0.01, so Whisper is not rate-sensitive over this range); the median rendered length is 1.001× the length asked for under the 44.1 kHz reading and would be 1.379× under the 32 kHz one, which an autoregressive decoder with a fixed token budget cannot do; and the spectrum shows no band-limit wall at 22 kHz, where a 32 kHz render relabelled to 44.1 would put one. The short clips are bimodal — a cluster at full length and a separate cluster at 0.1–0.4× — which is early end-of-audio emission, not a uniform rate error.

What this column therefore is, and is not. It is an honest measurement of the audio this path produced. It is not a verdict on MiniMax Music 3 as served: these renders come from an unmerged diffusers modular-pipeline port (diffusers 0.40.0.dev0), chosen because the usual serving stack has no minimax_music3 model, and the checkpoint's own shipped reference render is a 32 kHz file while its diffusers configs declare 44100. A runtime port that mis-stitches chunks or drives the latents out of distribution would look exactly like this. Read the column as MiniMax Music 3 via this pipeline, and do not generalise it.

The two conditions

Vocals only. A single voice and nothing else. For LeVo this is guaranteed by the renderer (above); for the other three it is asked for in the caption and measured afterwards. In all four arms the lyric is handed over as one continuous [verse] block with no chorus marker — a section boundary is where doubled and stacked vocals are learned to arrive — so the vocals-only / full-song contrast is the same manipulation in every arm.

Full song. The same lyric, in the lyric's own verse / chorus / bridge structure, prompted as an ordinary good song in the same genre. The caption in this condition says nothing at all about voices, choirs or instruments, in any of the four arms, and is byte-identical across the four.

What to listen for.
  • Is it one person? The vocals-only take should be a single voice from start to finish. Doubling, octave stacking and "ooh" pads are the usual failure, and no number on this page can catch them — the accompaniment column is blind to a second voice by construction.
  • Does the genre survive translation? The same style profile, the same caption, four languages, four models. Read a row straight across: where one model holds a language the others drop, that is the finding.
  • Did it sing the whole lyric? Several arms stop early. The lyric printed under each card is the full text; the grey tail is what was never reached by any arm.

Genre vocabularies: only one of the four has one

LeVo conditions its genre on a vocabulary of exactly 27 tags. Words outside it are not rejected — they are tokenised, conditioned on weakly, and the model falls back to its training prior, which is pop. None of our 20 genre names is one of those 27 tags, so each was anchored on the nearest in-vocabulary tag with the specific style words appended, and every card below carries a badge naming the tag that actually did the conditioning.

The other three have no closed genre vocabulary at all: HeartMuLa takes free comma-separated tags, ACE-Step a free caption of under 512 characters with a separate structured field, MiniMax a free prompt. They were nevertheless given the identical anchored caption, byte for byte, rather than the raw genre label they could have taken. That is deliberate: identical conditioning text is what makes the paired comparison a comparison. It also means the out-of-vocabulary penalty in the table below is LeVo's alone, and the other three are not credited for a freedom they were not allowed to use.

The language row is not decoration. LeVo 2 has no language conditioning whatsoever, ACE-Step has an explicit constrained one, and the other two infer it from the text. If the per-language tables show a model-by-language interaction, this row is the first place to look for why — it is a difference in architecture, not in prompting, and it was not something this comparison could equalise.

20 of the 20 genre labels are outside the 27 tags — that is all of them. The 10 anchors they were mapped onto — country, folk, hard rock, hip hop, pop, pop rock, R&B, rap, rock, soul — are all in the 27. So every row on this page is conditioned by a tag LeVo knows, plus a phrase it does not; the label in the card header is ours, and the badge on each card says which tag actually did the conditioning.

Where the lyrics come from. They are original compositions, written for this page from abstract genre style profiles — a target length, a section layout, a lexical-variety target, a point of view, a register and an emotional arc. Nothing else was given to the writer, and nothing else is claimed for them.

How to read a row

The page is grouped genre → style profile → language. Under each genre heading are its three style profiles; under each profile heading is the profile itself — the target length, lexical variety, register, point of view, section plan and emotional arc that the writer was given and nothing else — and then a row of four cards, the same profile written in English, German, French and Spanish. The four are meant to be read straight across.

Each card carries the language and genre in its header, a badge saying whether that genre name is in LeVo's vocabulary and what it was conditioned as if not, then eight players: the four models' vocals-only takes, then the four models' full-song takes, then the lyric. All eight sing exactly the same words. Beside every player are that clip's own numbers — length, accompaniment fraction, aesthetics, lyric word F1, and a mark when Whisper heard a language other than the intended one. Long lyrics are sung from the top and the audio stops partway; the text past that point is printed in grey and is in no clip.

Method

  • Held identical across the four arms. The words (each model sings the same clipped lines of the same lyric, in the same order); the caption text, byte for byte; the seed (crc32(clip_id), so one clip id has one seed everywhere); and the target duration, which is the length LeVo's language model chose for that lyric. Only the lyric separators differ, because the four checkpoints have incompatible input contracts: LeVo takes one line with  ;  between sections, the other three take one [tag] per line — MiniMax silently drops any text sharing a line with a leading tag.
  • LeVo 2. Batched, static KV cache, CUDA-graphed decode, batch 8; cfg 2.0, temperature 0.9, top_k 50. Caption budget 100 tokens and lyric budget 600, both truncated silently by x[:, :max_len]; every caption here was round-tripped through those tokenizers first and the longest is 18 of 100.
  • HeartMuLa 3B. HeartMuLa-oss-3B-happy-new-year with HeartCodec-oss, bf16 for the LM and fp32 for the codec (bf16 there degrades the audio), cfg 1.5, temperature 1.0, top_k 50, 12.5 Hz codec, 48 kHz out. Per-clip max_audio_length_ms set to the target duration.
  • ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo. acestep-v15-xl-turbo with the 5 Hz 4B language model planning bpm, key and structure; 8 sampler steps, no CFG (the model is distilled). dcw_enabled=False, set explicitly. It defaults to True — a wavelet-domain correction applied at every sampler step — and left at its default it destroys sung lyrics: measured Whisper F1 against the words handed to the model was 0.021 for the XL SFT checkpoint (a 30 s clip transcribes as the single word "so") and 0.605 for XL turbo, against 0.911 and 0.818 with it off. The flag's value is written into every timing record of this run so it can be checked rather than believed. use_cot_caption and use_cot_language are off so the planner cannot rewrite our caption — its rewrite adds instruments back — or re-guess the language.
  • MiniMax Music 3. The diffusers modular pipeline, bf16 on one GH200, 30 flow-matching steps per chunk, loaded from a local materialisation of the repo because the modular loader resolves every component through the Hub API even with a warm cache. Its vocoder reports 44.1 kHz although the model card says 32 kHz; the file is written at what the vocoder reports — and that was afterwards verified to be the correct reading of the samples, three independent ways, in the box above; the audio in this arm is not mislabelled. audio_duration is an upper bound only — the autoregressive model emits an end-of-audio token when it decides it is finished, which is why its length-compliance column reads as it does. The pipeline is an unmerged port and the column should be read as that pipeline's output, not as the model as served.
  • Which take is published. Three arms rendered 160 of their clips a second time at a different sample, to give the noise floor above. Those replicates are not a second chance at a nicer clip: the published take is the first one, and the replicate is substituted only when the first is defective by a test that never looks at any score — silent (RMS < 1e-4 or peak < 0.02) or shorter than 10 s. It fired for 11 MiniMax Music 3 clips — g01_0_de_vocal, g01_0_en_vocal, g02_0_fr_vocal, g03_0_en_vocal, g04_0_de_vocal, g10_0_de_vocal, g13_0_en_vocal, g16_0_de_vocal, g17_0_de_song, g17_0_fr_vocal, g18_0_es_song; every other clip on this page is a first take. Falling short of the requested duration is deliberately not counted as a defect: MiniMax treats the duration as an upper bound and stops when it decides it is done, so treating that as breakage would apply a length-maximising selection to one arm only, and the length table above is where that behaviour belongs.
  • Scoring. laion/music-aesthetics and laion/music-popularity-full-ft, both on laion/music-whisper embeddings, both consuming exactly 30 s at 16 kHz mono (centre crop for aesthetics, head crop for popularity, each card's own convention). Clips shorter than 30 s are zero-padded by the heads, which is why the length table is next to the score tables and not buried.
  • Separation. BS-Roformer Viperx ep.317 (SDR 12.9755), the same checkpoint as the earlier runs here, so the accompaniment fractions are comparable to them. The fraction is computed from the separator's own two stems as an energy partition, so it cannot go negative.
  • Audio. 160 kbps stereo mp3 in the dataset repo, one prefix per model (audio_lyrics_levo, audio_lyrics_heart, audio_lyrics_ace, audio_lyrics_minimax), referenced by absolute URL. Every player is preload="none".
  • Reuse. None was possible. Nothing previously rendered on this cluster used these lyrics — the earlier HeartMuLa, ACE-Step and MiniMax material was a different corpus in a different clip-id space with no overlapping clip id — so all 1,440 renders for the three added models were generated for this page, plus 640 seed replicates (160 per model, all four) for the noise floor. The 480 LeVo 2 clips were reused unchanged from the previous version of this page.

What is not measured here

  • Whether it is one voice. No number on this page can tell a solo from a doubled or harmonised vocal; a vocal separator keeps both inside the vocal stem. That judgement is left to the listener, and the page does not pretend otherwise.
  • Whether it is good. The aesthetics head is on record disagreeing with human judges by the width of the whole scale on this project's own clips, and the popularity head predicts a platform statistic, not quality.
  • Pronunciation. Whisper word F1 with the language forced rewards a model that produces recognisable words; it does not distinguish a native accent from a strong foreign one, and it is more forgiving of German and Spanish orthography than of French.

1920 clips scored, 36.44 GPU-hours of generation across the four models; LeVo 2 1.65 h over 480 of 640 renders; HeartMuLa 3B 11.87 h over 638 of 640 renders; ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo 3.62 h over 640 of 640 renders; MiniMax Music 3 19.30 h over 640 of 640 renders. Each figure is the generator's own per-clip wall time summed over the renders that carry a timing record, so a model whose record count is below its render count is under-counted rather than estimated — LeVo 2 batches eight clips to a GPU, which is why its seconds-per-clip is a fraction of the others'.
